notes.meaning: God warns that the life-giving rain Israel relied on would be replaced by blowing sand and dust. Hot winds would whip the dry, powdery earth into thick clouds that choke out green fields. Without water, crops wither and life in the land becomes impossible.

Instead of gaining victory, Israel would suffer terrible defeat before its enemies. The army would march out in orderly ranks in one direction, but flee in total panic in seven different directions. Surrounding nations would look upon their sudden downfall with shock and dread.

Fallen soldiers would be left lying out in the open instead of receiving an honorable burial. Birds of prey and wild animals would tear at the bodies, and no one would be left to drive them away. To the ancient Israelites, leaving a dead body unburied was one of the greatest shames imaginable.

The Lord warns that painful, incurable skin diseases would strike the people, similar to the boils Egypt suffered during the plagues. These ailments would include burning sores, severe scabs, and rashes that no medicine could heal. Such afflictions were a visible sign that God's protective care had been withdrawn.

Along with sickness in the body, the people would suffer deep distress of mind and spirit. Panic, confusion, and a lack of good sense would leave them unable to make wise choices. The sheer size of their disasters would leave them frozen in terror.

Even in the bright light of noon, the people would stumble around like someone who has lost their eyesight. Their plans and business ventures would fail, and invaders would rob them day after day. With no one to rescue them, they would live in constant helplessness.

A person would look forward to home and family, only to have every expectation ripped away by invaders. A man promised to be married would lose his bride to another, and those who built houses or planted vineyards would never enjoy them. Foreign enemies would step in and take everything just as it was ready.

Foreign soldiers would butcher farm animals right in front of the helpless owners. Invaders would slaughter the ox for food, haul away the donkey for army supplies, and seize the sheep. The owners would watch the loss of their livelihood without any power to stop it.

Conquerors would carry away young sons and daughters to be sold into slavery in distant nations. Parents would wear out their eyes weeping and watching the road, desperately hoping their children might return. They would have neither the strength to fight nor the wealth to buy them back.

A foreign nation with an unfamiliar language would sweep through the fields and eat the grain grown through hard labor. The Israelites would spend their lives under constant cruelty and unfair taxation. Watching strangers take the fruit of their sweat would leave families crushed and hungry.

The unending horrors of invasion, slavery, and robbery would push people past what their minds could handle. Seeing loved ones dragged away and homes ruined would drive parents to despair and madness. Sorrow would overwhelm their ability to think or hope.

Moses returns to the threat of physical suffering, describing agonizing, incurable boils breaking out on the knees and thighs. The painful sores would spread until they covered the body from the soles of the feet to the top of the head. This total physical misery was an outward sign of how deeply the nation was struck.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view this verse as a later addition or displacement because it returns to physical diseases after earlier verses had already moved on to military conquest.

notes.meaning: The people and the king they chose to rule over them would both be marched into exile by a distant empire. In that foreign land, they would be surrounded by lifeless idols carved from wood and stone. The false worship that had tempted them away from the true God would become their bitter prison.

In the nations where they were scattered, the people would become an example of total ruin. Other nations would use their name in jokes, insults, and expressions of disgust. Instead of enjoying honor as God's chosen people, they would face constant mockery.

Farmers would sow large bags of grain into the soil but reap only a tiny fraction at harvest time. Swarms of hungry locusts would strip the crops bare before the grain could ripen. Heavy work in the fields would yield almost nothing to eat.

People would plant and prune grapevines, looking forward to gathering baskets of sweet fruit and making wine. Instead, destructive worms and vineyard pests would chew through the stems and bunches. All the hard labor put into the vineyard would end in total loss.

Olive trees would grow all over the hills, yet families would not even have enough oil to rub on their skin. The olives would drop off the branches too early because of disease or blight, leaving the trees bare. A land known for rich olive oil would suddenly have none.

Parents would welcome sons and daughters into the world, but they would not get to watch them grow up at home. Invading armies would capture the young people and force them into exile as prisoners of war. The joy of family life would turn to grief as homes were emptied.

Swarms of buzzing insects would blanket the land and strip the trees and garden crops bare. Nothing green would escape their appetite. This complete loss of produce served as a clear sign of God's hand against their rebellion.

Foreigners living within Israel's towns—people who once had little status—would rise higher and higher in wealth and power. At the same time, the native Israelites would lose their property and sink lower and lower. The ordinary order of society would be completely turned on its head.

The resident foreigner would have enough wealth to lend money, while the impoverished Israelite would be forced to borrow. The outsider would lead like the head of a body, and Israel would follow like the tail. This reversed God's original promise that His obedient people would lead and lend to others.

Moses sums up that all these disasters would relentlessly pursue and overtake the people until their national life was crushed. This ruin would fall on them because they refused to listen to the LORD or keep the commands He gave. Turning away from God's covenant always leads to heartbreak and ruin.
